## Purpose

This SOP describes procedures for measuring soil temperature at multiple
depths to construct soil temperature profiles. Soil temperature
influences biological activity (microbial respiration, root growth, seed
germination), chemical reaction rates (nutrient mineralization,
decomposition), and physical processes (evaporation, frost heave)
[@ham2002; @hillel1998]. Temperature profiles are especially relevant
for photovoltaic panel studies, where shading alters the soil thermal
regime.

The amplitude and phase lag of diurnal and seasonal temperature waves
attenuate with depth according to the thermal diffusivity of the soil
profile, making multi-depth measurement essential for characterizing
subsurface energy budgets [@hillel1998]. Soil temperature also governs
rates of microbial respiration and nitrogen mineralization, with Q~10~
values typically ranging from 2 to 3 for the biologically active zone
[@onwuka2018]. When continuous monitoring is not feasible,
air-temperature-based models can be used to estimate soil temperature,
but these require site-specific calibration [@zheng1993].

## Scope

- **Applies to:** Spot measurements using handheld probe thermometers
  and continuous monitoring using datalogger-based thermocouple or
  thermistor systems at all EA Program field sites
- **Does not apply to:** Soil heat flux measurements (requires heat flux
  plates); fire-related soil heating studies
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites, including photovoltaic panel
  study areas, Bernard Field Station, and restoration sites

## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                        |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve monitoring plan, ensure training compliance   |
| Field Lead        | Coordinate installation, assign measurement schedules |
| Trained Personnel | Install sensors, collect data, maintain equipment     |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent measurement      |

## Definitions

- **Diurnal temperature variation:** The cycle of soil temperature
  change over a 24-hour period driven by solar radiation and radiative
  cooling; amplitude decreases with depth and is nearly zero below about
  50 cm in most soils.
- **Horizon temperature:** The temperature measured at a defined soil
  depth corresponding to a specific genetic horizon (e.g., A, B, C);
  used to characterize the thermal environment of the root zone and
  microbial communities.
- **Soil temperature:** The thermal energy state of the soil, expressed
  in °C; controls rates of microbial activity, organic matter
  decomposition, plant root growth, and soil gas fluxes.
- **Temperature gradient:** The rate of change in temperature with depth
  (°C cm^-1^); drives heat flux between soil layers and between the soil
  surface and the atmosphere.
- **Temperature profile:** A set of soil temperature measurements taken
  at multiple depths simultaneously or sequentially at a single
  location; used to characterize heat storage, heat flux, and seasonal
  thermal dynamics.
- **Thermistor:** A temperature sensor whose electrical resistance
  changes predictably with temperature; commonly used in data loggers
  for continuous soil temperature monitoring; requires calibration
  against a traceable reference thermometer.
- **Thermocouple:** A temperature sensor composed of two dissimilar
  metals joined at a measuring junction; produces a small voltage
  proportional to the temperature difference between the junction and a
  reference; used in handheld soil thermometers.

## Safety and Hazards

::: callout-warning
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Sharp probe tips, rebar stakes, hammering pilot holes in
  hard soil
- **Biological:** Ticks, snakes, and other field hazards (see SOP-F001)
- **Electrical:** Datalogger batteries and wiring (low voltage, minimal
  risk)
- **Environmental:** Heat exposure during summer measurements in
  southern California
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Gloves (when hammering pilot holes or handling rebar)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Safety glasses (when hammering)

### Required Training

- [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)

## Summary of Methods

Two approaches are described in this SOP. Select based on your project
requirements. Both methods are described in the SSSA Methods of Soil
Analysis [@ham2002]. The handheld method follows the GLOBE soil
temperature protocol [@globe2014soil], which has been widely adopted for
teaching and citizen-science applications.

| Method | Best For | Temporal Resolution | Cost |
|:-------------|:-------------|:----------------------------|:-------------|
| **Handheld probe** | Spot measurements, surveys across many points | Single time point per visit | Low |
| **Datalogger system** | Continuous monitoring, diurnal and seasonal patterns | Minutes to hours (automated) | High |

### Standard Measurement Depths

| Depth | Rationale |
|:---------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| 2 cm | Near-surface; responds rapidly to air temperature and solar radiation |
| 5 cm | Root zone surface; standard GLOBE protocol depth |
| 10 cm | Upper root zone; dampened diurnal signal |
| 20 cm | Mid root zone; minimal diurnal variation |
| 50 cm | Deep reference; seasonal variation only |

::: callout-tip
### Choosing Depths

For most EA Program projects, 5 cm and 10 cm are the minimum. Add 2 cm
for surface energy balance studies and 20 cm or 50 cm for deep profile
characterization.
:::

## Required Materials

### Method A: Handheld Probe

| Item | Notes |
|:---------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Thermocouple (Type T or Type K) or Resistance Temperature Detector (RTD) probes | Probe length must exceed deepest measurement depth + 2 cm. These probes carry a systematic measurement error; raw readings must be corrected using the probe-specific formula (see Data Correction under Data Management). |
| Electronic reader for probes | For the RTD probes, use either of the Omega HH804 readers. For the Type T probes, pair probe 1 with cable 1 and reader T819, and probe 3 with cable 2 and reader T299. The cable and reader both affect the reading, and the correction formulas are valid only for these specific equipment pairings. |
| Permanent marker, tape, or heat-shrink band | For marking measurement depths along the probe (see Prepare Depth Guide Marks) |
| Nail or awl | Same diameter as thermometer probe, for making pilot holes in hard soil |
| Hammer | For driving the nail into compacted soil |
| Field data sheet | Printed from Appendix A |
| Clipboard and pencil | Mechanical pencil preferred |
| GPS unit or smartphone | For recording measurement locations |
| Timer or watch | For tracking equilibration time |

### Method B: Datalogger System

| Item | Notes |
|:---------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Datalogger | Campbell Scientific CR1000, CR300, or equivalent |
| Thermocouple probes | Type T or Type E; one per measurement depth |
| Thermistor probes (alternative) | Campbell Scientific 109SS or equivalent |
| Averaging thermocouple probe (optional) | Campbell Scientific TCAV-L for energy balance studies |
| Soil temperature profiler (optional) | Hukseflux STP01 or METER TEROS 06 |
| Signal cable | Sufficient length from sensors to datalogger |
| Weatherproof enclosure | For datalogger and battery |
| 12V battery and solar panel | For continuous power |
| PVC conduit | For protecting cable runs |
| Shovel or soil knife | For sensor installation |
| Laptop with datalogger software | For programming and data download |

## Estimated Time

| Task | Time |
|:---------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Handheld: per measurement point (all depths) | 10--15 minutes (including equilibration) |
| Datalogger: initial installation | 2--4 hours per station |
| Datalogger: data download visit | 15--30 minutes |
| Datalogger: sensor replacement | 30--60 minutes |

## Procedure: Method A -- Handheld Probe

### Prepare Depth Guide Marks

Before going to the field, mark each measurement depth directly on the
probe. The temperature sensor is at the tip of the probe, so each mark
is placed at the target depth measured from the tip. In the field, push
the probe in until the mark for the target depth is level with the soil
surface.

| Target Depth | Mark Distance from Tip |
|:-------------|:-----------------------|
| 5 cm         | 5 cm                   |
| 10 cm        | 10 cm                  |
| 20 cm        | 20 cm                  |

Use a permanent marker, a wrap of tape, or a heat-shrink band at each
depth. Verify the marks against a ruler before each field season, since
tape and marker can shift or wear off with use.

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Photo of a probe with tape marking the measurement depths -->

<!-- Save as: images/soil_temp_probe_depth.jpg -->

### Select Measurement Locations

1.  Navigate to the predetermined sampling location and record GPS
    coordinates
2.  Select a representative spot with undisturbed soil surface
3.  Gently brush away surface litter without disturbing the mineral soil

### Take Measurements

1.  If the soil is hard, use the nail and hammer to make a pilot hole to
    the target depth. Make the hole the same diameter as the probe to
    ensure good thermal contact.
2.  Insert the probe and gently push until the mark for the target depth
    is level with the soil surface
3.  Wait at least 2 minutes for the probe to equilibrate with the soil.
    Equilibration time depends on the thermal conductivity of the soil
    and the thermal mass of the probe; dry sandy soils may require 5
    minutes or longer [@ham1992].
4.  Read the temperature every 1 minute until two consecutive readings
    are within 0.5 C of each other
5.  Record the stabilized temperature, depth, time, and location on the
    data sheet
6.  Remove the probe and repeat at the next depth in the same hole (work
    from shallowest to deepest)
7.  Move to the next measurement location

::: callout-important
### Equilibration Is Essential

Do not rush readings. An un-equilibrated probe will read too warm in
cool soil and too cool in warm soil. Two minutes is the minimum; 3--5
minutes may be needed in dry or very cold soil.
:::

### Timing

- For comparable data across sites, complete all measurements within 1
  hour of local solar noon (approximately 12:00--13:00 PST)
- For diurnal profiles, measure at consistent intervals (e.g., every
  2--3 hours over a 24-hour period)
- Record the exact time of each measurement

## Procedure: Method B -- Datalogger System

### Sensor Installation

1.  Select a representative location and record GPS coordinates
2.  Dig a narrow trench or pit to the deepest sensor depth on one side
    of the measurement point (do not disturb the soil column directly
    above the sensors)
3.  Insert sensors horizontally into the undisturbed soil wall at each
    target depth, pressing firmly to ensure good thermal contact
4.  Backfill the trench carefully, maintaining the original soil
    layering as much as possible
5.  Route cables through PVC conduit to the datalogger enclosure
6.  Mark the sensor locations with discreet, flush-to-ground markers

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Cross-section diagram showing sensors inserted horizontally into a trench wall at multiple depths -->

<!-- Save as: images/soil_temp_sensor_installation.jpg -->

::: callout-note
### Settling Period

Soil disturbed during installation needs time to return to
representative thermal conditions. Allow a minimum of 48 hours before
using data for analysis. One to two weeks is ideal for deep sensors.
:::

### Datalogger Programming

1.  Connect all sensors to the datalogger following the wiring diagram
    for your sensor type
2.  Program the datalogger to scan sensors at the desired interval
    (typically every 1--5 minutes)
3.  Configure storage to record averages at 15-minute or 30-minute
    intervals
4.  Set the datalogger clock to local standard time (do not use daylight
    saving time)
5.  Verify readings against a calibrated handheld thermometer at 5 cm
    depth

### Data Download

1.  Visit the station at regular intervals (weekly to monthly, depending
    on battery and storage capacity)
2.  Connect a laptop and download data using the manufacturer's software
3.  Check for gaps, sensor failures, or anomalous readings in the field
4.  Transfer data to the project database within 48 hours

## Calibration

### Handheld Probes

1.  Prepare an ice-water bath (crushed ice + deionized water, stirred);
    this should read 0.0 C
2.  Insert the probe and allow to equilibrate for 3 minutes
3.  Record the reading; it should be within 0.5 C of 0.0 C
4.  If outside tolerance, adjust or replace the thermometer
5.  Calibrate before each field season and after any suspected damage

The ice-point calibration is a single-point check; for research
requiring higher accuracy, a two-point calibration (ice-water and
warm-water bath at approximately 40 C) is recommended [@ham2002].

::: callout-tip
### Type K Probes

Type K probes require a multi-point calibration to build their
error-correction formula. Measure the reading at a minimum of three
temperatures: an ice bath (approximately 0 C), room temperature, and a
heating plate at approximately 50 C. Use a reference thermometer at each
point and fit the correction from the paired readings (see Data
Correction).
:::

### Datalogger Sensors

1.  Before installation, place all sensors in a well-stirred water bath
2.  Record readings from all sensors simultaneously
3.  All sensors should agree within 0.3 C
4.  Document any offsets and apply corrections in post-processing if
    needed

## Quality Control

- Calibrate all thermometers and sensors before each field season
- For handheld measurements, take readings at a minimum of 3 replicate
  locations per plot
- Record the time of every measurement (soil temperature changes
  throughout the day)
- For datalogger systems, inspect data weekly for drift, gaps, and
  anomalous values
- Include a surface air temperature measurement alongside soil
  temperatures for context
- Photograph each measurement location at the start of each season

## Data Management

### Handheld Data

Enter data from field sheets into the project spreadsheet within 48
hours. Required fields:

- Date, time (local standard time), site, plot ID, observer
- Measurement depth (cm)
- Temperature (C)
- Surface condition (bare soil, litter, vegetated, shaded)
- Notes (e.g., soil was saturated, recent rain)

### Data Correction

The handheld probes carry a systematic measurement error, so raw
readings must be corrected before analysis. Apply the calibration
formula matched to the specific probe, cable, and reader combination;
the corrections below are valid only for the equipment pairings listed.
Let $T_\text{raw}$ be the reading in °C and $T_\text{corr}$ the
corrected temperature in °C.

**RTD Probe 1**

$$T_\text{corr} = 1.160\,T_\text{raw} - 13.23$$

**RTD Probe 2**

$$T_\text{corr} = 1.167\,T_\text{raw} - 14.609$$

**Type T Probe 1 (Cable 1, reader T819)**

$$T_\text{corr} = 1.028\,T_\text{raw} - 8.797$$

**Type T Probe 3 (Cable 2, reader T299)**

$$T_\text{corr} = 1.004\,T_\text{raw} - 8.121$$

Record which probe, cable, and reader were used for each measurement so
the correct formula can be applied during processing. Type K probes must
be calibrated and corrected using a formula derived from their own
three-point calibration (see Calibration).

### Datalogger Data

- Download raw files and archive unmodified copies
- Process data into a standardized format: timestamp, site, depth,
  temperature
- Flag and document any corrections (sensor offsets, gap-filling)
- Store processed data in the project database with metadata

## Waste and Site Impact

- Minimize soil disturbance during installation; backfill trenches
  carefully
- Remove all temporary equipment, flagging, and markers after the study
- Leave permanent sensors in place for long-term monitoring unless the
  study is complete
- Pack out all trash and supplies

## Training Record

Before measuring soil temperature independently, personnel must:

1.  Read this SOP and [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)
    in full
2.  Calibrate a handheld probe using an ice-water bath
3.  Demonstrate proper use of depth marks and equilibration timing
4.  For datalogger work: demonstrate sensor installation, datalogger
    programming, and data download under supervision
5.  Be signed off by the field lead or PI
